message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is not legal advice; if you need help with a specific situation, consider consulting an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months’ rent for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (e.g., unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear).
• Landlords must provide a written itemized statement of deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease, move‑in inspection report, and any receipts for repairs you pay.
• Request a written receipt for the deposit when you hand it over. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | • Texas law requires landlords to keep premises safe and habitable (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity).
• If the landlord fails to make necessary repairs, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or terminate the lease (see “Repair & Deduct” below). | • Document problems with photos and written notices.
• Give the landlord a reasonable amount of time to fix issues before taking further action. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For month‑to‑month leases: 30‑day written notice to end tenancy.
• For fixed‑term leases: the lease term ends automatically unless you give notice to renew or the landlord gives notice to terminate. | • Keep copies of all notices sent and received. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas Property Code §92.001‑92.006.
• Common grounds: non‑payment of rent, lease violations, or the landlord’s intent to sell or demolish the property.
• The landlord must serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease termination).
• If you fail to comply, the landlord can file an unlawful detainer action in court. | • Respond promptly to any notices.
• If you receive an eviction notice, you have the right to contest it in court. | | **Repair & Deduct** | • Under Texas Property Code §92.004, you may repair a problem and deduct the cost from your rent if:
 1. The landlord has failed to repair after notice.
 2. You have given written notice and a reasonable time to fix.
 3. The repair cost is reasonable and you keep receipts. | • Keep receipts and a written record of the repair. | | **Rent Control / Rent Increases** | • Texas has no statewide rent‑control laws. Landlords can raise rent at the end of a lease term or with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month). | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the Fair Housing Act and Texas Property Code §92.001, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, family status, or source of income. | • Report discrimination to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Privacy / Entry** | • Landlords must give reasonable notice (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries and check that the landlord follows notice rules. | | **Lease Termination & Early Move‑Out** | • If you break a lease early, you may be liable for rent until a new tenant is found, unless the landlord can prove they made reasonable efforts to re‑rent. | • Offer to help find a replacement tenant or negotiate a release. | | **Legal Resources** | • Texas Attorney General’s Office – Consumer Protection Division
• Texas Legal Services Center
• Local tenant‑rights groups (e.g., Texas Tenants Union)
• HUD’s Fair Housing Hotline | • Contact these resources if you need legal representation or guidance. | ### Quick Checklist for Your Next Move 1. **Read your lease carefully** – note any clauses about rent increases, repairs, or termination. 2. **Document everything** – photos, written notices, receipts. 3. **Give proper notice** – 30 days for month‑to‑month, 3 days for non‑payment. 4. **Know your rights** – you can withhold rent only after giving notice and waiting a reasonable period. 5. **Seek help if needed** – use the resources above for disputes or legal advice. --- If you’d like a sample lease or a more detailed contract tailored to your situation, let me know and I can generate one for you.
